Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-09
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Dr. Elisa Romero (CTO), Ravi Shah (Head of ML), Kendra Li (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be incomplete):
GrayCrane is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + dedicated usage. Primary constraints are p95 latency targets for streaming use cases (chat-like assistants inside clinicians' UI), plus throughput during nightly batch annotation jobs. They asked about p95 numbers, how batching and KV cache affect token/sec, and private VPC options for PHI. Redwood team to provide benchmark harness and pricing options; customer to provide prompt set and traffic trace for pilot.

Topics: p95 streaming latency, concurrency targets, tokens/sec benchmarking, Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) tradeoffs, SOC2/KMS/audit concerns, fallback strategies and quantization optioning

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya, account lead for Redwood, and with me is Jonas from our SRE/SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Elisa: Hi, I'm Elisa, CTO at GrayCrane, thanks for setting this up. We're curious about how Redwood will behave under our mixed load.
[00:11] Ravi: Hey, Ravi here. Head of ML. We have low-latency clinical assistant flows and also nightly bulk processing where throughput matters.
[00:18] Kendra: Kendra, platform. I'll be focused on VPC/network and data residency.
[00:21] Jonas: Thanks, great. Quick agenda: p95 targets you care about, concurrency, streaming token/sec numbers, and deployment options (Hosted/Dedicated/Private). We'll then map a pilot benchmark. Does that sound right?
[00:30] Elisa: Yep. I'll start with the requirements: for clinician chat we want p95 <= 450ms from user request to first token on average for a 1k token response streaming case, and steady-state token throughput doesn't need to be huge — more like 30-60 qps — but spikes can hit 250 concurrent streams. For nightly jobs we need to sustain ~2000 tokens/sec across a fleet for batch inference.
[00:50] Maya: Okay that's super helpful. A couple clarifying Qs — when you say 1k token response, is that total tokens generated or including prompt tokens?
[00:58] Ravi: Total generation tokens. Prompts vary but are usually 200-400 tokens. So end-to-end 1k generation, streamed.
[01:06] Jonas: Cool. A few quick notes: p95 streaming latency tends to be more sensitive to prefix caching, KV cache locality, and how continuous batching is configured. On Hosted we can usually hit sub-500ms p95 for many open models with streaming enabled, but at 250 concurrent streams you'll want Dedicated and tuned batching policies.
[01:28] Elisa: When you say "sub-500ms" is that per-token or first-token? We care about time-to-first-token mostly.
[01:33] Jonas: First-token. When I reference p95 400-500ms that's time-to-first-token for models we've tuned with micro-batching and optimized kernels on A100-like hardware. For throughput numbers like tokens/sec, that depends on model size + quantization. For instance a 13B quantized path might do 700-1200 tokens/sec per GPU in throughput mode, whereas streaming latency per stream is driven by concurrency scheduling.
[01:55] Ravi: Do you have numbers for 70B style models? We have some high-quality generation needs.
[02:00] Jonas: For 70B families, latency is usually higher — first token p95 often in the 700ms-1.2s range on Hosted unless you commit Dedicated capacity and use memory-optimized instances + q4 quantization strategies. We can also provide half-precision kernels and batched KV cache warmups.
[02:16] Kendra: On Private/VPC — we need SOC2, KMS-integration with our HSM, and audit logs for all token payloads. Is that supported?
[02:25] Maya: Yes, on Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, SAML SSO, RBAC and full audit logs. Hosted also is SOC2 compliant and we can provide SOC2 report, but for HSM and specific key control you'd be looking at Private.
[02:38] Elisa: For data residency we may need the inference inside our VPC. Is there a hybrid story — e.g., control plane hosted, inference nodes in our VPC?
[02:46] Jonas: Absolutely. That's the Private control plane model: control plane managed by Redwood but inference in your VPC or on-prem, with the same API surface. We recommend that for PHI workflows. Latency is then dominated by your network hops, but you get full key control.
[02:59] Ravi: Back to the p95 numbers — you mentioned batching policies and KV cache. Can you walk through a realistic config for 250 concurrent streams and 1k token outputs?
[03:08] Jonas: Sure. Typical setup: Dedicated pool with autoscale headroom (we usually recommend reserving ~30-40% spare capacity to absorb spikes). Configure continuous batching with a max-batch size tuned to keep time-to-first-token under your target — in practice that's a trade: larger batches improve token/sec and lower unit cost but increase tail latency. For streaming-first-token targets, we set aggressive micro-batching thresholds (e.g., 4-10ms wait or small batch size) so the first-token goes out fast, and then we aggregate for later tokens. Also enable prefix caching so repeated system prompts are cached in GPU memory (reduces KV workload).
[03:41] Maya: I'll add that Redwood Optimize can recommend batching thresholds based on your traffic pattern. For your nightly batch jobs instead you'd flip to larger batching for throughput.
[03:50] Elisa: Can you quantify the cost/latency trade? If we move from Hosted to Dedicated how does that change p95 and cost?
[03:58] Maya: Hosted is simpler and often cheaper at low-to-medium volume. Dedicated increases predictability — you'll hit lower variance in p95 and can tune kernels. As a rough example, Hosted streaming p95 for a 13B model might be ~350-450ms at low concurrency; Dedicated at same load and with reserved GPUs and optimized kernels could bring p95 down to ~250-350ms and give you more consistent tails under burst. Cost is higher for Dedicated due to reserved GPU cost but you get predictable throughput and the option to use custom quantization profiles. We'll send a modeled cost sheet that shows breakpoints where Dedicated becomes cheaper per-token.
[04:31] Ravi: For benchmark setup, can you provide a harness? We need something reproducible. Also we use sodium-coded prompts and maintain some proprietary tokenization; does your harness allow plugging in our tokenizer?
[04:41] Jonas: Yes, our benchmark harness includes a client that can be swapped to your tokenizer. We'll provide a Dockerized script with load scenarios: steady-state 60 qps, 250 concurrent streaming spikes, and a batch throughput mode. It will collect p50/p95/p99 for time-to-first-token and per-token latency, and tokens/sec.
[05:00] Kendra: About quantization — are those lossy for our clinical phrasing? We cannot tolerate hallucinations introduced by aggressive quantization.
[05:07] Jonas: Good point. We recommend running quality regressions as part of the benchmark. Redwood Optimize includes suggested quant profiles (e.g., q4_0, q5) and we track simple n-gram overlap and a small eval set. For clinical safety you probably want conservative quantization or keep the model in higher precision for critical responses.
[05:24] Elisa: What about fallbacks — if Dedicated pool is saturated, can requests transparently fall back to Hosted or a smaller model? We need graceful degradation to keep UIs responsive.
[05:33] Maya: Yes, smart routing policies support fallback by region/tier/model. You can set a policy to fallback to a smaller model with lower latency or to a hosted pool. We'll annotate the SLA differences in the routing policy.
[05:44] Ravi: For tokens/sec profiling, do you measure per-GPU tokens/sec and end-to-end throughput including network and serialization overheads?
[05:51] Jonas: We capture both. The harness measures model-side token emission rate (GPU) and end-to-end client-observed tokens/sec including muxing and streaming overhead. We'll highlight where the bottleneck is — e.g., kernel vs network vs batching logic.
[06:05] Kendra: On networking, what's the expected egress and bandwidth footprint for streaming 250 concurrent users with 1k tokens? Rough calc shows big egress.
[06:13] Maya: Correct — 250 concurrent streams * 1k tokens is 250k tokens in flight; bandwidth depends on token size and whether streaming compresses text. We can give a bandwidth model and show how prefix caching reduces duplicated data across requests.
[06:26] Elisa: Security check — do you support SAML for login and can we restrict who can start dedicated pools?
[06:31] Maya: Yes SAML, role-based access control, and we can lock pool creation behind RBAC and org-level approvals.
[06:37] Ravi: For the pilot, what's realistic? We want Redwood to run a 2-hour window where we ramp concurrency to 250 and run a batch throughput run overnight.
[06:46] Jonas: That works. Suggested plan: 1) baseline Hosted test with your prompt set; 2) Dedicated reserve for 2 hours with ramp scenario; 3) Batch throughput overnight on Dedicated. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. We'll also run a conservative quantization run and a no-quant run for quality comparison.
[07:05] Elisa: How invasive is it to use Private? We have procurement constraints, so Hosted is faster procurement-wise but Private gives the KMS control we need.
[07:14] Maya: Procurement for Hosted is quick — sign-up, set org billing. Private requires SOW and some networking work but we have a template and can do a staged migration: start Hosted, run benchmark, then move inference into your VPC if required.
[07:27] Kendra: One last thing — audit logs retention and access — we need 3-year retention for compliance. Can Redwood support that?
[07:33] Maya: Hosted audit log retention is configurable, and for enterprises we offer long-term retention add-ons. On Private you control log retention in your own storage. We'll attach the audit log SLA in the followup.
[07:44] Elisa: Great. Any competitor comparisons we should be aware of? We trialed Anthropic but had trouble with throughput and OpenAI rate limits.
[07:52] Jonas: Noted. From a throughput and private deployment standpoint, Redwood's Dedicated and Private options aim to be more flexible than purely hosted providers and more production-oriented than just kernel-level runtimes. We'll highlight that in the follow-up.
[08:03] Maya: Okay let's do a quick walk-through of the benchmark scripts and metrics — Jonas, can you outline the script steps?
[08:10] Jonas: Sure — script does: 1) handshake + warmup (populate KV cache) 2) steady-state streaming traffic at 60 qps for 15m 3) spike ramp to 250 concurrent streams over 10 minutes and hold for 30m 4) cool-down 5) batch throughput test (multiple async requests to saturate GPUs) 6) quality eval runs comparing baseline to quantized outputs. We collect time-to-first-token, per-token latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and network egress.
[08:38] Ravi: For warmup, how long to fill KV cache for long prompts?
[08:42] Jonas: Usually a few iterations — 2-5 warmups per unique system prompt is enough to get cache hot. We'll advise you on warmup sequences in the harness.
[08:50] Kendra: Are there telemetry hooks? We need to send traces to our existing observability.
[08:54] Maya: Yes we provide tracing hooks and can forward traces to your Datadog/Elastic stack; also per-token cost/latency breakdowns in Console.
[09:02] Elisa: Okay recap — send benchmark harness, pricing, SOC2 and KMS docs, and schedule pilot.
[09:09] Maya: Correct. Jonas — anything to add?
[09:11] Jonas: I'll upload the harness and a README with the expected inputs (prompt set, tokenizer, traffic trace) and a recommended Dedicated pool config for your scenario.
[09:19] Ravi: One quick nit — can we test a multi-region failover? Clinician traffic is US-east primary but we need low seconds-level failover to EU.
[09:27] Jonas: We can simulate region failover in the pilot by routing a portion of traffic to another region and measuring added latency. Our smart routing will allow you to define runbooks.
[09:35] Kendra: Procurement-wise we'll need an SOW and estimated MRR for Dedicated.
[09:40] Maya: We'll include a preliminary SOW and a 30/60/90 day pricing projection.
[09:44] Elisa: Perfect. thanks all.
